picks.reasoning: Strip the narrative and G2 simply have the better players in more lanes, with Caps the best individual on the Rift in this game and a mid pool deep enough to turn that into early leads. LOS have real dangers in Ackerman's playmaking and Duduhh's late-game Kai'Sa, and G2 love to hand back leads, but one good fight doesn't erase a skill gap across the map, so I'm backing the stronger players.

usedLessons.text: Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but in a Bo1 I have to check whether the star's lane can actually turn that edge into a lead before I treat it as the whole argument. When the opposing team has a proven jungle-support duo that can steal a messy game, I should rate that duo as skill too, not dismiss it as chaos, and I should be more skeptical of a Viper-sized edge when the whole BLG team is the one the crowd is backing. (from Swiss BLG vs MKOI; picked BLG, actual MKOI 1-0)

Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but I overrated one star and ignored the matchup around him: a jungler's edge only counts if his lanes give him something to work with, and POUT showed that a top laner who can win his own lane and take over fights can cancel it. Next time I'll compare the players across all five roles, and when the whole board agrees on one side, I'll take that as a reason to look harder at the other team's best individual, not as comfort. (from Swiss TLAW vs CFO; picked TLAW, actual CFO 1-0)

Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but it wins by turning into early leads, so I should check whether the stronger players, especially mid and jungle, have draft pools deep enough to get those leads and keep them. Next time I'll back the skill gap on those specific matchups instead of leaning on the region gap, which only confirms what the players already show. (from Swiss HLE vs TES; picked HLE, actual HLE 1-0)

Top lesson: Skill won again, because DK had the better player in more lanes and Smash outplayed everyone, so one star like Caps can't outweigh a talent edge across the map. Keep judging the matchup player by player, leave region talk out unless the report flags a big gap, and ignore the "2-0 in their heads" vibes the crowd loves. (from Swiss G2 vs DK; picked DK, actual DK 1-0)

Pantheon can skirmish and the first dragon is a real flip trigger, and G2 did hand DK a lead in their Worlds opener, so I'm not going higher. But if G2 win the first tower and herald and LOS can't force early fights, the Ryze draft never gets its window.

When the upset path I name is built on the opponent's comfort picks, I should cut my confidence until the draft shows BLG can deny or punish them, and not lean on league strength unless the report flags a big gap. usedLessons.text: Support lesson: I read BLG's chemistry as a strength and MKOI's youth as fragility, but a team that has been blown out internationally and has nothing to lose can play loose and unified, so I should weigh how a team's mood actually shows up in its recent games rather than leaning on a narrative like "hungry after an MSI final" or "young and shaky." Support lesson: When I read a team's chemistry and morale, I should weigh what I see in the actual game against my read of their character. CFO's past collapses were evidence about their mood, but the chemistry call only holds if I also check the current signals, like roster stability, how they were playing lately, and whether those lead-throwing games were still shaping their confidence. I'll keep trusting that the team decides it, but I'll hold my read of a side's nerves more loosely and lower my confidence when the story I'm telling is one every other analyst also tells.
